claim: The response of a category-selective region in VTC can be computed as the degree to which the low-level properties of the stimulus match a category template.
source: Here, we show that the response of a category-selective region in VTC can be computed as the degree to which the low-level properties of the stimulus match a category template.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Template model described in the manuscript and its cross-validation performance shown in Figure 2b.

claim: During execution of a task, the bottom-up representation in VTC is scaled by the intraparietal sulcus (IPS).
source: Moreover, we show that during execution of a task, the bottom-up representation is scaled by the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), and that the level of IPS engagement reflects the cognitive demands of the task.
evidence: The claim is supported by the IPS-scaling model and experimental data showing correlation between IPS activity and VTC modulation (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: The level of IPS engagement reflects the cognitive demands of the task.
source: Moreover, we show that during execution of a task, the bottom-up representation is scaled by the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), and that the level of IPS engagement reflects the cognitive demands of the task.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Drift diffusion model showing that IPS activity increases with reaction time, which reflects task difficulty (Figure 6).

claim: The visual word form area (VWFA) selectively responds to words.
source: We focus on two specific VTC regions, the visual word form area (VWFA), which selectively responds to words (Cohen et al., 2000, 2002; Wandell et al., 2012), and the fusiform face area (FFA), which selectively responds to faces (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The fusiform face area (FFA) selectively responds to faces.
source: We focus on two specific VTC regions, the visual word form area (VWFA), which selectively responds to words (Cohen et al., 2000, 2002; Wandell et al., 2012), and the fusiform face area (FFA), which selectively responds to faces (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The response to a word in VWFA is 2.4 times stronger when the word is presented at 100% contrast as compared to 3% contrast.
source: For example, the response to a word in VWFA is 2.4 times stronger when the word is presented at 100% contrast as compared to 3% contrast.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Both image contrast and phase coherence modulate response amplitudes in VWFA and FFA.
source: However, we find that responses are not invariant to low-level properties of the stimulus: both image contrast and phase coherence modulate response amplitudes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Responses in VWFA and FFA are larger for the categorization and one-back tasks compared to the fixation task.
source: Responses are larger for the categorization (Figure 1d, green lines) and one-back tasks (Figure 1d, blue lines) compared to the fixation task (Figure 1d, red lines), and we interpret these response increases as reflecting top-down modulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The VWFA response to 3%-contrast words during the one-back task exceeds the response to 100%-contrast words during the fixation task.
source: For example, the VWFA response to 3%-contrast words during the one-back task exceeds the response to 100%-contrast words.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Task effects in lower-level areas exist but are smaller in size than in VWFA and FFA.
source: Task effects in lower-level areas exist but are smaller in size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Template model accurately predicts a large amount of variance in the responses of VWFA and FFA during the fixation task.
source: Applying the Template model to responses measured during the fixation task, we find that the Template model accurately predicts a large amount of variance in the responses of VWFA and FFA (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The Template model outperforms a phenomenological Category model that posits that perceived stimulus category is sufficient to predict the response of category-selective regions.
source: The model outperforms a phenomenological model, termed the Category model, that posits that perceived stimulus category is sufficient to predict the response of category-selective regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation performance comparison shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Responses to non-preferred stimuli are meaningful and the result of a well-defined computation performed by the visual system.
source: This suggests that responses to non-preferred stimuli are meaningful and the result of a well-defined computation performed by the visual system (Haxby et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Template model's ability to predict non-preferred responses and is supported by citation.

claim: The Template model outperforms simplified versions that include only one of the two processing stages.
source: The model also outperforms simplified versions of the Template model that include only one of the two processing stages, as well as versions of the Template model in which the category template lacks tuning (non-selective template), is equally weighted between words and faces (mixed template), or is constructed randomly (random template) (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 2c.

claim: High-level representations are built from, and fundamentally tied to, low-level properties through a series of linear and nonlinear operations.
source: The present results indicate that although high-level representations are not identical to low-level properties, they are built from, and fundamentally tied to, low-level properties through a series of linear and nonlinear operations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Template model architecture and its performance.

claim: The categorization and one-back tasks act as a scaling mechanism on the representation observed during the fixation task.
source: Importantly, we observe that the categorization and one-back tasks act as a scaling mechanism on the representation observed during the fixation task.
evidence: The claim is supported by visualization of neural responses in multi-dimensional space shown in Figure 3.

claim: The amount of scaling is not constant across stimuli but is stimulus-specific.
source: Moreover, the amount of scaling is not constant across stimuli but is stimulus-specific, and this is most evident when considering the lowest contrast stimuli (Figure 3, black dots).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Substantial responses to non-preferred categories are present in each ROI and these responses are scaled during the stimulus-directed tasks.
source: The visualization also shows that substantial responses to non-preferred categories are present in each ROI (for example, faces in VWFA, words in FFA) and that these responses are scaled during the stimulus-directed tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Information regarding non-preferred categories is present in each ROI and is actively modulated when subjects perform a perceptual task on those categories.
source: Thus, not only is information regarding non-preferred categories present in each ROI, but this information is actively modulated when subjects perform a perceptual task on those categories.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that non-preferred category responses are scaled during tasks.

claim: Response scaling occurs even for non-preferred stimulus categories, and the amount of scaling varies as a function of stimulus properties such as image contrast.
source: Rather, response scaling occurs even for non-preferred stimulus categories, and the amount of scaling varies as a function of stimulus properties such as image contrast.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3b and 3c.

claim: The scaling induced by the stimulus-directed tasks serves to increase the distance of neural responses from a linear decision boundary that separates words and faces.
source: For example, assuming that one use of the stimulus representation in VTC is to discriminate whether the presented stimulus is a word or face (or, more generally, identify the category of the stimulus [DiCarlo et al., 2012]), the scaling induced by the stimulus-directed tasks serves to increase the distance of neural responses from a linear decision boundary that separates words and faces (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3d and involves inference about the functional role of scaling.

claim: The categorization and one-back tasks appear to act via the same scaling mechanism.
source: Interestingly, the categorization and one-back tasks appear to act via the same scaling mechanism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both tasks produce similar scaling patterns in Figure 3.

claim: Top-down cognitive processes do not impart additional tuning or selectivity but serve to amplify the selectivity that is already computed by visual cortex.
source: These results suggest that, at least for the perceptual tasks sampled here and the spatial scale of neural activity measured in this study, top-down cognitive processes do not impart additional tuning or selectivity but serve to amplify the selectivity that is already computed by visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the scaling mechanism observed in the data.

claim: Responses in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) predict the top-down enhancement of VTC responses better than responses in any other region of cortex.
source: Applying this connectivity analysis to our data, we find that responses in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) predict the top-down enhancement of VTC responses (Figure 4b) better than responses in any other region of cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The source of top-down modulation is localized to the IPS-0 and IPS-1 subdivisions of the IPS.
source: Comparing our results to a publicly available atlas (Wang et al., 2015), we estimate that the source of top-down modulation is localized to the IPS-0 and IPS-1 subdivisions of the IPS (see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with an anatomical atlas and connectivity analysis results.

claim: The vertical occipital fasciculus (VOF) connects the VWFA and FFA with the functionally identified peak region in the IPS.
source: Using diffusion-weighted MRI and tractography (data acquired in 8 of 9 subjects), we show that the VOF specifically connects the VWFA and FFA with the functionally identified peak region in the IPS (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by diffusion MRI tractography data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The VWFA falls within the ventral terminations of the VOF for seven subjects.
source: The VWFA falls within the ventral terminations of the VOF for seven subjects and, for the eighth, the VWFA is 2.7 mm anterior to the VOF, well within the margin of error for tractography (Jeurissen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by tractography data and citation regarding tractography error margins.

claim: The FFA falls within the ventral terminations of the VOF for all eight subjects.
source: The FFA falls within the ventral terminations of the VOF for all eight subjects.
evidence: The claim is supported by tractography data.

claim: The IPS-scaling model accurately characterizes the observed data.
source: We find that the IPS-scaling model accurately characterizes the observed data (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The IPS-scaling model uses a single set of scale and offset parameters on the IPS response and accurately predicts scaling of VTC responses across the categorization and one-back tasks.
source: Importantly, the IPS-scaling model uses a single set of scale and offset parameters on the IPS response and accurately predicts scaling of VTC responses across the categorization and one-back tasks (Figure 5b, top plot).
evidence: The claim is supported by model results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The scaling of VTC by IPS is a general mechanism supporting perception and is independent of the specific cognitive task performed by the observer.
source: This finding suggests that the scaling of VTC by IPS is a general mechanism supporting perception and is independent of the specific cognitive task performed by the observer.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that a single set of parameters works across tasks.

claim: When IPS exhibits close to zero evoked activity, the corresponding scaling factor is close to one.
source: Furthermore, the scale and offset parameters that are estimated from the data show that when IPS exhibits close to zero evoked activity (for example, FACE at 100%-contrast; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), the corresponding scaling factor is close to one.
evidence: The claim is supported by parameter estimates from the IPS-scaling model.

claim: A phenomenological scaling model outperforms a phenomenological additive model in describing VTC responses.
source: We find that a phenomenological scaling model (Scaling model (task-specific)) outperforms a phenomenological additive model (Additive model (task-specific)), confirming earlier observations that the top-down modulation is a scaling effect (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The IPS interacts with VTC multiplicatively rather than additively.
source: This conclusion is further supported by the higher performance observed when the IPS interacts with VTC multiplicatively (IPS-scaling model) compared to when it interacts additively (IPS-additive model).
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Top-down modulation from the IPS is dependent on the stimulus and task.
source: Finally, we find that the performance of the IPS-scaling model degrades if the IPS input into the model is shuffled across conditions (IPS-scaling model (shuffle, shuffle within task)), confirming that top-down modulation from the IPS is dependent on the stimulus and task.
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The Drift diffusion model predicts reaction times measured in the categorization task with high quality.
source: First, we use VTC responses during the fixation task (reflecting sensory evidence) to predict reaction times measured in the categorization task. The quality of the predictions is quite high (Figure 6b, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The cross-validated predictions of the Drift diffusion model explain substantial variance in IPS.
source: The cross-validated predictions of our proposed model explain substantial variance in IPS (Figure 6b, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Categorization of low-contrast stimuli is difficult because the IPS computations required to perform the task involve longer accumulation time.
source: According to the model, categorization of low-contrast stimuli is difficult because the IPS computations required to perform the task involve longer accumulation time, and this is reflected in the fact that IPS response magnitudes increase monotonically with reaction time.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Drift diffusion model and supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Top-down modulation of VTC by IPS is a direct consequence of fulfilling task demands.
source: Thus, our model performs several critical functions: it relates the cognitive task performed by the subject to IPS activity, proposes a computational explanation of task difficulty, and posits that top-down modulation of VTC by IPS is a direct consequence of fulfilling task demands.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the integrated model architecture.

claim: A template operation on low-level visual properties generates a bottom-up stimulus representation in VTC.
source: In summary, we have measured and modeled how bottom-up and top-down factors shape responses in word- and face-selective cortex. A template operation on low-level visual properties generates a bottom-up stimulus representation, while top-down modulation from the IPS scales this representation in the service of the behavioral goals of the observer.
evidence: The claim summarizes the Template model findings.

claim: Top-down modulation from the IPS scales the bottom-up representation in the service of the behavioral goals of the observer.
source: In summary, we have measured and modeled how bottom-up and top-down factors shape responses in word- and face-selective cortex. A template operation on low-level visual properties generates a bottom-up stimulus representation, while top-down modulation from the IPS scales this representation in the service of the behavioral goals of the observer.
evidence: The claim summarizes the IPS-scaling model findings.

claim: The Template model does not capture the step-like response profile of VTC as phase coherence is varied.
source: For instance, the Template model does not capture the step-like response profile of VTC as phase coherence is varied (see Figure 2b), and the accuracy with which the model accounts for a wide range of stimuli that includes faces, animals, and objects, is moderate at best (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the model based on comparison with data.

claim: The accuracy with which the Template model accounts for a wide range of stimuli that includes faces, animals, and objects is moderate at best.
source: For instance, the Template model does not capture the step-like response profile of VTC as phase coherence is varied (see Figure 2b), and the accuracy with which the model accounts for a wide range of stimuli that includes faces, animals, and objects, is moderate at best (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the model based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When subjects perform the fixation task, the contrast-response function (CRF) in VWFA is monotonically increasing.
source: When subjects perform the fixation task, the contrast-response function (CRF) in VWFA is monotonically increasing, whereas during the one-back task, the CRF flips in sign and is monotonically decreasing (see Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: During the one-back task, the contrast-response function in VWFA flips in sign and is monotonically decreasing.
source: When subjects perform the fixation task, the contrast-response function (CRF) in VWFA is monotonically increasing, whereas during the one-back task, the CRF flips in sign and is monotonically decreasing (see Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: IPS has been identified as playing a key role in controlling spatial attention.
source: Previous research has identified IPS as playing a key role in controlling spatial attention (Saalmann et al., 2007; Lauritzen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Despite the fact that spatial attention is always directed towards the foveal stimulus during the categorization and one-back tasks, the amount of modulation from the IPS is flexible and varies depending on properties of the stimulus and demands of the task.
source: Our results extend these findings by showing that, despite the fact that spatial attention is always directed towards the foveal stimulus during the categorization and one-back tasks, the amount of modulation from the IPS is flexible and varies depending on properties of the stimulus and demands of the task.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing stimulus-specific scaling.

claim: During the categorization task, the observed enhancement for low-contrast stimuli is much larger than that for high-contrast stimuli.
source: For example, during the categorization task, the observed enhancement for low-contrast stimuli is much larger than that for high-contrast stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Difficult tasks enhance visual responses.
source: This mechanism could explain the finding that difficult tasks enhance visual responses (Ress et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and inference from the model.

claim: The direct influence of IPS on neural responses in VTC is consistent with anatomical measurements demonstrating the existence of the vertical occipital fasciculus (VOF).
source: The direct influence of IPS on neural responses in VTC is consistent with anatomical measurements demonstrating the existence of a large white-matter pathway connecting dorsal and ventral visual cortex, called the vertical occipital fasciculus (VOF) (Yeatman et al., 2013, 2014; Takemura et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The response-gain model posits that attention causes a multiplicative scaling of contrast-response functions.
source: The response-gain model (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999) posits that attention causes a multiplicative scaling of contrast-response functions.
evidence: The claim describes a model from previous literature.

claim: The contrast-gain model posits that attention causes a leftward shift of contrast-response functions.
source: The contrast-gain model (Reynolds et al., 2000) posits that attention causes a leftward shift of contrast-response functions (as if contrast were increased).
evidence: The claim describes a model from previous literature.

claim: The additive-shift model posits that attention causes an additive increment to contrast-response functions.
source: Finally, the additive-shift model (Buracas and Boynton, 2007) posits that attention causes an additive increment to contrast-response functions; we find that our observations are better explained by a scaling, not additive, mechanism (see Figures 3 and 5c).
evidence: The claim describes a model from previous literature.

claim: Previous models of attention cannot explain the effects reported in this study.
source: Thus, the effects we report are novel, and previous models of attention cannot explain these effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of the current findings with previous models.

claim: Sensory information arrives at VTC, these signals are routed to IPS for evidence accumulation, and then feedback from the IPS modulates the VTC response.
source: Our working hypothesis is that sensory information arrives at VTC (as indexed by fixation responses), these signals are routed to IPS for evidence accumulation, and then feedback from the IPS modulates the VTC response (as indexed by categorization and one-back responses).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the model architecture and data.

claim: The IPS may be inducing a scaling on neural activity in VTC or a sustainment of neural activity in VTC.
source: Second, the scaling of BOLD response amplitudes by IPS is consistent with at least two potential mechanisms at neural level: the IPS may be inducing a scaling on neural activity in VTC or, alternatively, a sustainment of neural activity in VTC.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing alternative mechanisms.

claim: ECoG responses in FFA exhibit sustained activity that is linked to long reaction times in a face gender discrimination task.
source: Some support for the latter comes from a recent study demonstrating that ECoG responses in FFA exhibit sustained activity that is linked to long reaction times in a face gender discrimination task (Ghuman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: IPS is part of larger brain networks involved in attention and decision-making.
source: Finally, IPS is part of larger brain networks involved in attention (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002) and decision-making (Gold and Shadlen, 2007), and identifying the computational roles of other regions in these networks is necessary for a comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms of perception.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Eleven subjects participated in this study.
source: Eleven subjects participated in this study.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Two subjects were excluded due to inability to identify VWFA in one subject and low signal-to-noise ratio in another subject, leaving a total of nine usable subjects.
source: Two subjects were excluded due to inability to identify VWFA in one subject and low signal-to-noise ratio in another subject, leaving a total of nine usable subjects (age range 25–32; six males, three females).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: All subjects were healthy right-handed monolingual native-English speakers, had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity, and were naive to the purposes of the experiment.
source: All subjects were healthy right-handed monolingual native-English speakers, had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity, and were naive to the purposes of the experiment.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about subject characteristics.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Washington University in St. Louis Institutional Review Board.
source: Informed written consent was obtained from all subjects, and the experimental protocol was approved by the Washington University in St. Louis Institutional Review Board.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Stimuli were small grayscale images (approximately 2° × 2°) presented at fixation.
source: All stimuli were small grayscale images (approximately 2° × 2°) presented at fixation.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about stimulus properties.

claim: Each stimulus type consisted of 10 distinct images.
source: Each stimulus type consisted of 10 distinct images (for example, 10 different faces for a face stimulus), and a subset of these images were presented on each given trial.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about stimulus design.

claim: Stimuli were presented in 4 s trials, one stimulus per trial.
source: Stimuli were presented in 4 s trials, one stimulus per trial.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about trial design.

claim: In a trial, four images from a given stimulus type were presented sequentially using an 800 ms ON, 200 ms OFF duty cycle.
source: In a trial, four images from a given stimulus type (for example, FACE, 10% contrast) were presented sequentially using an 800 ms ON, 200 ms OFF duty cycle.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about trial design.

claim: A small dot (0.12° × 0.12°) was present at the center of the display throughout stimulus presentation.
source: Throughout stimulus presentation, a small dot (0.12° × 0.12°) was present at the center of the display.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design.

claim: The dot switched to a new randomly selected color every 600 ms using a set of six possible colors.
source: The dot switched to a new randomly selected color every 600 ms using a set of six possible colors: magenta, red, yellow, green, cyan, and blue.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design.

claim: Each run began and ended with a 16 s baseline period in which no stimuli were presented.
source: Each run began and ended with a 16 s baseline period in which no stimuli were presented.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design.

claim: Each run lasted 344 s (5.7 min).
source: Each run lasted 344 s (5.7 min).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design.

claim: Subjects performed each of the three tasks four times during the course of the experiment, yielding a total of 12 runs.
source: Subjects performed each of the three tasks four times during the course of the experiment, yielding a total of 3 tasks × 4 runs = 12 runs.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design.

claim: The physical stimulus sequence was held constant across tasks.
source: The physical stimulus sequence (including the temporal ordering of stimulus images and dot colors) was held constant across tasks.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about experimental design.

claim: MRI data were collected at the Neuroimaging Laboratory at the Washington University in St. Louis School of Medicine using a modified 3T Siemens Skyra scanner and a 32-channel RF coil.
source: MRI data were collected at the Neuroimaging Laboratory at the Washington University in St. Louis School of Medicine using a modified 3T Siemens Skyra scanner and a 32-channel RF coil.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about data acquisition.

claim: For functional data, 28 oblique slices covering occipitotemporal cortex were defined.
source: For functional data, 28 oblique slices covering occipitotemporal cortex were defined: slice thickness 2.5 mm, slice gap 0 mm, field-of-view 200 mm × 200 mm, phase-encode direction anterior-posterior.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about data acquisition parameters.

claim: A whole-brain version of the protocol involving 58 slices and a multiband factor of 2 was used in three of the nine subjects.
source: To achieve comprehensive coverage for localization of top-down effects, a whole-brain version of the protocol involving 58 slices and a multiband (Feinberg et al., 2010) factor of 2 was used in three of the nine subjects.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about data acquisition.

claim: Diffusion data were not acquired for one subject due to time constraints.
source: Diffusion data were not acquired for one subject due to time constraints.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about data acquisition.

claim: Subjects were highly consistent in their category judgments: for each stimulus, the most frequently reported category was the same across subjects and was reported more than 85% of the time.
source: Subjects were highly consistent in their judgments: for each stimulus, the most frequently reported category was the same across subjects and was reported more than 85% of the time.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: The pre-processed fMRI data were analyzed using GLMdenoise, a data-driven denoising method.
source: The pre-processed fMRI data were analyzed using GLMdenoise (Kay et al., 2013a) (http://kendrickkay.net/GLMdenoise/), a data-driven denoising method that derives estimates of correlated noise from the data and incorporates these estimates as nuisance regressors in a general linear model (GLM) analysis of the data.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about data analysis methods.

claim: Visual field maps were defined using the population receptive field (pRF) technique applied to retinotopic mapping data.
source: Visual field maps were defined using the population receptive field (pRF) technique applied to retinotopic mapping data (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Kay et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about ROI definition methods.

claim: FFA was defined as face-selective cortex located on the fusiform gyrus.
source: We defined FFA as face-selective cortex (responses to faces greater than the average response to the other three categories) located on the fusiform gyrus.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about ROI definition.

claim: VWFA was defined as word-selective cortex located in and around the left occipitotemporal sulcus.
source: We defined VWFA as word-selective cortex (responses to words greater than the average response to the other three categories) located in and around the left occipitotemporal sulcus.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about ROI definition.

claim: The Template model is almost certainly an oversimplification of the complex nonlinear processing performed in VTC.
source: The present model, termed the Template model, is almost certainly an oversimplification of the complex nonlinear processing performed in VTC.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of model limitations.

claim: The Template model is theoretically motivated, consistent with hierarchical theories of visual processing.
source: Nevertheless, the model is theoretically motivated, consistent with hierarchical theories of visual processing (Fukushima, 1980; Heeger et al., 1996; Serre et al., 2007; DiCarlo et al., 2012; Rolls, 2012), and provides a useful starting point for characterizing the computations that underlie word- and face-selectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: The Template model is parsimonious with only three free parameters.
source: Moreover, unlike recently popular deep neural network models that also involve hierarchical processing (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Yamins et al., 2014; Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015), the model we propose is parsimonious with only three free parameters, and is therefore straightforward to fit and interpret (see Figure 2a and Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about model properties.

claim: The first stage of the Template model involves computing a V1-like representation of the image using isotropic Gabor filters.
source: The first stage of the Template model involves computing a V1-like representation of the image. The image is first resized to 250 pixels × 250 pixels, and luminance values are mapped to the range [–0.5,0.5], which has the effect of mapping the gray background to 0. The model then calculates V1 energy in the same way as the SOC model (Kay et al., 2013c). Specifically, the image is projected onto a set of isotropic Gabor filters occurring at eight orientations, two quadrature phases, and a range of positions (63 x-positions × 63 y-positions).
evidence: The claim is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: The second stage of the Template model involves taking the V1-like representation of the image and comparing it to a category template to generate the predicted response.
source: The second stage of the Template model involves taking the V1-like representation of the image and comparing it to a category template to generate the predicted response.
evidence: The claim is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: Category templates were constructed from the WORD and FACE stimuli at 100% contrast.
source: Given that we do not have sufficient sampling of stimuli to directly estimate templates from the data (but see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we adopted the simple strategy of constructing templates from our stimulus set. Specifically, we took the WORD and FACE stimuli at 100% contrast and used the first stage of the Template model to compute a V1-like representation of these stimuli.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about model implementation.

claim: Using a category template constructed from the face stimuli guarantees that the face stimuli produce large responses from the model.
source: Because the category template is constructed from the same stimuli used in our experiment, it is guaranteed that the Template model predicts large responses to the preferred category (for example, using a category template constructed from the face stimuli guarantees that the face stimuli produce large responses from the model).
evidence: The claim is a logical inference from the model construction.

claim: There is no guarantee that the Template model will accurately account for responses to the other stimuli used in the experiment.
source: However, there is no guarantee that the model will accurately account for responses to the other stimuli used in our experiment.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference about model limitations.

claim: The IPS-scaling model multiplies the bottom-up response in VTC measured during the fixation task by a scaled version of the IPS response observed during a stimulus-directed task.
source: The IPS-scaling model multiplies the bottom-up response in VTC measured during the fixation task by a scaled version of the IPS response observed during a stimulus-directed task
evidence: The claim is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: The Drift diffusion model accepts as input fixation responses in VTC and produces as output predicted reaction times and IPS responses for the categorization task.
source: The model accepts as input fixation responses in VTC and produces as output predicted reaction times and IPS responses for the categorization task.
evidence: The claim is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: VTC responses provide evidence regarding which stimulus category has been presented to the subject, and this evidence is accumulated over time by the IPS in order to make a final decision regarding stimulus category.
source: The basic idea is that VTC responses provide evidence regarding which stimulus category has been presented to the subject, and this evidence is accumulated over time by the IPS in order to make a final decision regarding stimulus category.
evidence: The claim is a description of the conceptual basis of the Drift diffusion model.

claim: The instantiation of the drift diffusion model is relatively simple, as it is non-stochastic and does not characterize trial-to-trial variability.
source: Note that our instantiation of the drift diffusion model is relatively simple, as it is non-stochastic and does not characterize trial-to-trial variability. Thus, it can be viewed as a simplified version of the classic drift diffusion model (Ratcliff, 1978).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about model properties.

claim: Neuronal responses in parietal cortex reflect the duration of the decision-making process.
source: Given that neuronal responses in parietal cortex reflect the duration of the decision-making process (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001), we can use RT to predict IPS activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.
